title: Chicken vs Turkey vs Pork vs Beef: Protein, Fat and Calories

seo.title: Chicken vs Turkey vs Pork vs Beef Nutrition
seo.meta_description: Compare lean chicken, turkey, pork and beef by protein, fat, calories and iron per 100 grams, with practical serving context.
seo.search_intent: Compare common meats using similar lean cuts.

excerpt: Chicken and turkey breast are the leanest examples, but pork tenderloin can be close. Lean beef supplies more heme iron, and cut choice often matters more than the animal name.
content_html:
Comparing chicken, turkey, pork and beef only by species is misleading because cuts vary widely. Skinless chicken breast and skin-on thigh are different foods nutritionally; pork tenderloin and bacon are even farther apart. A useful comparison uses lean cooked cuts that could fill a similar role on the plate.

Nutrition per 100 g cooked

CutProteinFatCaloriesIron
Skinless chicken breast~31 g~3.6 g~165~1 mg
Skinless turkey breast~29.5 g~2 g~145~1 mg
Lean pork tenderloin/loin~27 g~5 g~165~1 mg
Lean beef round~29 g~6 g~185~2.5 mg

Protein

Chicken breast is about 31 g protein/100 g versus roughly 29.5 g for turkey breast. In a 5-ounce / 142 g serving, that is about 44 g versus 42 g — a small difference.

Lean beef can also be around 29 g/100 g, with lean pork near 27 g. All four are concentrated protein foods when lean cuts are chosen.

Fat and calories

The turkey example has about 2 g fat and 145 calories/100 g; chicken 3.6 g and 165 calories; pork 5 g and 165 calories; lean beef 6 g and 185 calories.

Fat provides 9 calories per gram compared with 4 for protein or carbohydrate, so fattier cuts increase calories quickly.

The cut matters more than the species label

Bacon can exceed 40–50 g fat/100 g, while pork tenderloin may be near 5 g. Skin-on chicken thighs also contain substantially more fat than skinless breast.

Calling all pork fatty or all chicken lean hides these differences.

Iron

Lean beef has a clear advantage in iron: commonly around 2–3 mg/100 g versus roughly 1 mg in lean chicken, turkey or pork. Meat also provides heme iron, which is generally absorbed more efficiently than nonheme iron.

B vitamins

Beef is a strong vitamin B12 source; pork is particularly rich in thiamin; chicken and turkey provide substantial niacin and vitamin B6. Similar protein numbers do not mean identical micronutrient profiles.

Fresh vs processed

Fresh turkey breast is not nutritionally equivalent to deli turkey. Processed products can contain added water, sodium and other ingredients. The table compares minimally processed meat.

Most protein for the fewest calories

Turkey and chicken breast are especially efficient. Turkey provides about 29.5 g protein for 145 calories/100 g, while the lean beef example provides about 29 g for 185 calories. Protein is almost the same, but energy differs by around 40 calories/100 g.

Choosing between them

For very low fat, turkey or chicken breast are easy choices. For more iron and B12, beef stands out. For a lean alternative to poultry, pork tenderloin can be close to chicken in calories.

Cooking method can change the final plate more than the meat choice: one tablespoon of oil adds roughly 120 calories in the U.S. tablespoon measure.

Bottom line

There is no universal winner. Lean cuts of all four provide substantial protein. Chicken and turkey are especially lean, beef provides more iron, and lean pork can be much lighter than its reputation suggests.

Sources

Values are based on representative entries in USDA FoodData Central.

faq.question: Which has more protein, chicken or turkey?
faq.answer: Cooked chicken breast is about 31 g/100 g and turkey breast about 29.5 g/100 g; the difference is small.

faq.question: Is pork always fattier than chicken?
faq.answer: No. Pork tenderloin can be around 5 g fat/100 g, while bacon can exceed 40–50 g/100 g.

faq.question: Which meat has more iron?
faq.answer: Lean beef generally has the most among these examples, around 2–3 mg/100 g versus about 1 mg in lean poultry and pork.
